# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical reading: Varden and Halden 24-month follow-up

## Overall verdict

This is the most useful document of the five. It does what the earlier ones called for:

- **It uses stricter measurement.** Hours are taken from system log-ins as well as timesheets.
- **It runs a registered confirmatory test.** The meetings hypothesis is tested under a plan filed before the 24-month results existed.
- **It holds the earlier claims to account, fairly.** It shows the review's four long-run studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which is the concern I raised about the "no decay" claim. And a randomised, record-based, log-hours gain of 8.5% at 24 months directly answers the claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact."

There are still four problems worth taking seriously:

- the Summary overstates the decline by comparing two different measures;
- the log-hours measure is not clearly defined and doesn't fit with the meetings data;
- a simple accounting calculation suggests meetings explain much more than 47% of the gain;
- the control arm was contaminated from month 15, which the 24-month estimate does not address.

## Arithmetic

The main figures check out:

- **Per-hour gain on timesheets:** 0.966 ÷ 0.88 gives +9.8%.
- **Per-hour gain on logs:** 0.966 ÷ 0.89 gives +8.5%.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 ÷ 40.3 is 0.866, and 96.8 ÷ 0.866 gives +11.8%.
- **Counter-office staffing:** an 83% hours ratio times a 6.7% per-hour gain implies about 13% more staff needed to restore output, close to the county's 12%.

## Main problems

### 1. The Summary compares two different measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But the 12.5% is based on timesheets, and the 8.5% on system logs. The like-for-like comparison is **12.5% to 9.8%**, which the body of the paper reports correctly.

Even that decline is uncertain. The confidence intervals (6.9 to 18.4, and 4.6 to 15.2) overlap almost completely. The data are consistent with some fading, but also with none. Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" should carry that caveat.

### 2. The log-hours measure needs defining, and it doesn't fit the meetings data

**Is there a baseline?** The paper says log-in time was "added" at follow-up. A difference-in-differences estimate (−11%) needs pre-trial log data. The paper should say whether the system kept historical log-in records. If it didn't, the −11% is just a treated-versus-control comparison at 24 months, without the before-and-after adjustment used everywhere else.

**What does it count?** It is described as time "working on cases." If it excludes meetings, the numbers don't fit together. Taking the baseline of about 37.9 timesheet hours and the 12% fall:

| | Total hours | Meeting hours | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated, baseline | ~37.9 | 7.4 | ~30.5 |
| Treated, 24 months | ~33.4 | 3.9 | ~29.5 |
| **Change** | **−4.5** | **−3.5** | **about −1.0 (−3%)** |

Time on cases can't fall by 11% if all non-meeting time fell by only about 3%. So either the log measure includes time logged in during meetings, or the figures are inconsistent.

The answer matters for the mediation analysis. If logged hours include meeting time, cutting meetings raises output per hour partly by arithmetic. If they exclude it, meetings must work through some other channel, such as fewer interruptions.

### 3. A simple accounting suggests meetings explain nearly all of the gain, not 47%

Using the paper's baseline meeting figures (treated 7.4 to 3.9; control 7.2 to 7.0), the treated offices' non-meeting time fell by about 1.2 hours relative to control. That is roughly 4%. Over the same period, output per employee fell by 3.4%.

That puts **output per non-meeting hour at roughly 0%, or about +0.6%**. On this accounting, staff worked at the same pace when not in meetings. Essentially all of the per-hour gain comes from removing meeting time from the denominator.

This doesn't make the registered mediation analysis wrong. The two methods measure different things:

- the **accounting** is a decomposition of averages;
- the **mediation** uses differences between offices and assumes no unmeasured confounding.

But the gap between "about 100%" and "47%" is large, and the paper should explain it. It also matters for interpretation. If the accounting is closer to the truth, the 35% "unexplained" share and the 18% attributed to fatigue largely disappear.

**Caveat:** this calculation uses the 9-month baseline of 37.9 hours and assumes timesheets include meeting time. It is rough, but a ~2-point error in either figure would not change the conclusion.

### 4. The control arm was contaminated from month 15

Two of the seven control offices cut their meetings by 2.1 hours a week and gained about 4.1% in output per hour. This means part of the control group received a version of the treatment's main mechanism for the last nine months. That pushes the 24-month estimate **toward zero**, and may account for some of the apparent decline from 9.8% to 12.5%.

The paper needs a sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices. It reports the meeting audit as a curiosity, but it never connects it to its own estimate of decline.

The audit result is also consistent with the accounting above. If meetings produced nothing, removing 2.1 hours from about 37.6 would give roughly +5.9% per hour, close to the observed +4.1%. The usual caveats apply: two offices, no comparison group, and possible regression to the mean.

### 5. Weaknesses in the mediation test

- **Office-months are not independent.** The paper credits "a larger sample of office-months," but repeated months from the same 14 offices add little information. The effective sample is 14 clusters. A 95% CI of 28% to 66% looks narrow for that, and the paper doesn't say how clustering was handled.
- **The registration may not be fully independent of the exploratory finding.** The plan was filed at month 11, after the exploratory meetings finding at month six. If the confirmatory test uses office-months from before month 11, part of it re-tests the data that generated the hypothesis. The paper should restrict the test to months 12 to 24, or show that it did.
- **The two mediators are probably linked.** Fewer meetings may reduce fatigue. A model that treats the two as separate shares (47% + 18%) may misattribute part of the meetings effect to fatigue.

## Smaller points

- **The Halden reversions don't fit the paper's own category.** The Summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations." But the marketing agency cited client deadlines. That is deadline-bound discretionary work, not coverage-bound work. It suggests a third category (externally paced deadline work), not a clean confirmation of the coverage distinction.
- **Some outcomes are missing.**
  - *Backlogs against statutory deadlines.* The 9-month report flagged these; with output per employee still down 3.4%, they should be reported.
  - *Overtime and labour costs* for case-processing offices.
  - *The 24-month estimation window.* It is unclear whether the estimate is cumulative or covers only the final months.
- **The Halden subset is double-selected,** and the response rate was 14 of 23. The paper's "upper bound" framing is appropriate. Three of 14 reverted (21%), against 5 of 61 (8%) in the original pilot, so reversion continued after the six-month evaluation.
- **One author ran the original Halden pilot.** The working paper misreported the timing of withdrawals. That doesn't affect the Varden results, but readers should note it when assessing the Halden section.
- **Fatigue moved differently in the two sources.** It improved by 0.34 SD in Varden at 24 months, while Halden's energy measure decayed. These are different measures in different populations, and the paper is right not to equate them.

## Updated synthesis across all five documents

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Is there a genuine per-hour gain in discretionary work? | Yes. About 8.5–10% at 24 months on randomised, record-based, log-measured evidence. |
| Does it fade? | Possibly a little (12.5% to 9.8%, CIs overlapping). The decline may be partly due to control-arm contamination. It does not vanish. |
| Does output per worker hold up? | Not quite. About −3 to −4%, consistent with the review's controlled estimate. Unit labour costs rise. |
| Coverage-bound work? | Fails without extra staff. Varden ended this arm at month 12. Restoring service would need about 12% more staff and about 9% higher cost per contact. |
| Mechanism? | Mostly fewer meetings. Simple accounting suggests most or all of the gain; the registered mediation says about half. Fatigue plays a smaller role. |
| Does the hours cut cause the gain, or just prompt reorganisation? | Unknown, and now the key question. The control-office meeting audit hints that much of the gain may be available without cutting hours. No study has a "reorganise but keep full hours" arm. |

The next study worth running would compare three arms: reduced hours, a meeting-and-workflow audit at full hours, and an unchanged control. Without that, an employer can't tell whether it is buying a productivity gain or paying for a reorganisation it could have done anyway.
